steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a sound and complete projection operator for multiparty session types based on automata. Cover the background on protocol verification and MSTs, the problem with existing projection operators, and our contributions and evaluation.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:

  - most verification problems (e.g. deadlock freedom) undecidable (cite)

  - multiparty session types (MSTs) (cite), much attention recently; survey by Ancona et al. (cite)

  - local implementations: behavior per role
  - implementability: exists collection of local implementations whose composite behavior, as a communicating state machine (CSM), matches global type and is deadlock-free
  - synthesis: compute such implementation from implementable global type

- Projection operators
  - MST approaches solve synthesis + implementability together via efficient syntactic projection operator (cite)
  - projection operator = partial map global types -> collections of implementations
  - proj sound: every \mathbf{G} in domain implemented by \texttt{proj}(\mathbf{G}); complete: every implementable global type in domain
  - existing practical operators: all incomplete (or unsound)
  - recent: implementability decidable for a class of MSTs, reduction to safe realizability of globally cooperative HMSCs (cite)
  - in principle complete + sound operator for that class, but not practical: check is in EXPSPACE

- Contributions
  - first practical sound and complete projection operator for general MSTs
  - synthesis conceptually easy (cite); challenge = deciding implementability
  - separate synthesis from checking implementability
  - standard automata-theoretic construction -> candidate implementation (even for non-implementable global type)
  - unlike prior work (cite): verify candidate directly with efficiently checkable conditions from the global type
  - non-implementable: constructive completeness proof gives counterexample trace

- Complexity
  - resulting operator -> PSPACE decision procedure for implementability
  - generalizes and tightens earlier decidability/complexity results (cite)

- Evaluation
  - prototype evaluated on benchmarks from the literature
  - combines efficiency of lightweight incomplete syntactic projection (cite) with generality of heavyweight automata-based model checking (cite)
  - handles protocols rejected by previous practical approaches, keeps efficiency that makes MST techniques attractive

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Communication protocols are key parts of many safety and operation critical systems, which makes them prime targets for formal verification. But most verification problems for these protocols (e.g. deadlock freedom) are undecidable. Several restrictions have been proposed so that verification becomes computationally tractable. Multiparty session types (MSTs) in particular have got a lot of attention in recent years (see, e.g., the survey by Ancona et al.). In MSTs a protocol is specified as a global type, and the global type describes the desired interactions of all the roles in the protocol. Local implementations describe the behaviors for each individual role. The implementability problem for a global type asks if there is a collection of local implementations whose composite behavior, when viewed as a communicating state machine (CSM), matches the behavior of the global type and is deadlock-free. The synthesis problem is to compute such an implementation from a global type that is implementable.

Approaches based on MSTs usually solve synthesis and implementability at the same time with an efficient syntactic projection operator. Abstractly, a projection operator is a partial map from global types to collections of implementations. A projection operator proj is sound when every global type \mathbf{G} in its domain is implemented by \texttt{proj}(\mathbf{G}), and it is complete when every implementable global type is in its domain. All the existing practical projection operators for MSTs are incomplete (or they are unsound). Recently it was shown that the implementability problem is decidable for a class of MSTs, using a reduction to safe realizability of globally cooperative high-level message sequence charts (HMSCs). In principle this result gives a complete and sound projection operator for this class. But this operator would not be practical. In particular the implementability check that is proposed is in EXPSPACE.

  - first practical sound and complete projection operator for general MSTs

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Communication protocols are key parts of many safety and operation critical systems, which makes them prime targets for formal verification. But most verification problems for these protocols (e.g. deadlock freedom) are undecidable. Several restrictions have been proposed so that verification becomes computationally tractable. Multiparty session types (MSTs) in particular have got a lot of attention in recent years (see, e.g., the survey by Ancona et al.). In MSTs a protocol is specified as a global type, and the global type describes the desired interactions of all the roles in the protocol. Local implementations describe the behaviors for each individual role. The implementability problem for a global type asks if there is a collection of local implementations whose composite behavior, when viewed as a communicating state machine (CSM), matches the behavior of the global type and is deadlock-free. The synthesis problem is to compute such an implementation from a global type that is implementable.

Approaches based on MSTs usually solve synthesis and implementability at the same time with an efficient syntactic projection operator. Abstractly, a projection operator is a partial map from global types to collections of implementations. A projection operator proj is sound when every global type \mathbf{G} in its domain is implemented by \texttt{proj}(\mathbf{G}), and it is complete when every implementable global type is in its domain. All the existing practical projection operators for MSTs are incomplete (or they are unsound). Recently it was shown that the implementability problem is decidable for a class of MSTs, using a reduction to safe realizability of globally cooperative high-level message sequence charts (HMSCs). In principle this result gives a complete and sound projection operator for this class. But this operator would not be practical. In particular the implementability check that is proposed is in EXPSPACE.

Contributions. In this paper we present the first projection operator for general MSTs that is practical and also sound and complete. Synthesis for implementable global types is conceptually easy - the hard part is to determine if a global type is implementable or not. So we separate synthesis from checking implementability. First we use a standard automata-theoretic construction to get a candidate implementation for a global type that may not be implementable. Then, unlike the previous decidability work, we verify that this implementation is correct directly, using conditions that are derived from the global type and can be checked efficiently. If a global type is not implementable, our completeness proof is constructive and gives a counterexample trace.

The projection operator we get gives a PSPACE decision procedure for implementability. This result generalizes the decidability and complexity results obtained in the earlier work and also tightens them.

We evaluate a prototype of our projection algorithm on benchmarks that we took from the literature. Our prototype gets the benefits of both the efficiency of the existing syntactic projection operators, which are lightweight but incomplete, and the generality of the heavyweight model checking techniques based on automata: it handles protocols that were rejected by the previous practical approaches and it still keeps the efficiency that makes MST-based techniques so attractive.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Communication protocols are key components in many safety and operation critical systems, which makes them prime targets for formal verification. Unfortunately, most verification problems for such protocols (e.g. deadlock freedom) are undecidable [1]. Several restrictions have been proposed to make verification computationally tractable [2,3,4,5,6,7]. In particular, multiparty session types (MSTs) [8] have garnered a lot of attention in recent years (see, e.g., the survey by Ancona et al. [9]). In the MST setting, a protocol is specified as a global type, which describes the desired interactions of all roles involved in the protocol. Local implementations describe the behaviors of each individual role. The implementability problem for a global type asks whether there exists a collection of local implementations whose composite behavior, when viewed as a communicating state machine (CSM), matches that of the global type and is deadlock-free. The synthesis problem is to compute such an implementation from an implementable global type.

MST-based approaches typically solve synthesis and implementability simultaneously via an efficient syntactic projection operator [8,10,11,12]. Abstractly, a projection operator is a partial map from global types to collections of implementations. A projection operator proj is sound when every global type \mathbf{G} in its domain is implemented by \texttt{proj}(\mathbf{G}), and complete when every implementable global type is in its domain. Existing practical projection operators for MSTs are all incomplete (or unsound). Recently, the implementability problem was shown to be decidable for a class of MSTs via a reduction to safe realizability of globally cooperative high-level message sequence charts (HMSCs) [13]. In principle, this yields a complete and sound projection operator for the considered class. However, such an operator would not be practical: in particular, the proposed implementability check is in EXPSPACE.

Contributions. In this paper, we present the first practical sound and complete projection operator for general MSTs. The synthesis problem for implementable global types is conceptually easy [13] – the challenge lies in determining whether a global type is implementable at all. We therefore separate synthesis from checking implementability. We first use a standard automata-theoretic construction to obtain a candidate implementation for a potentially non-implementable global type. Unlike [13], however, we then verify the correctness of this implementation directly, using efficiently checkable conditions derived from the global type. When a global type is not implementable, our constructive completeness proof yields a counterexample trace.

The resulting projection operator gives a PSPACE decision procedure for implementability. This result both generalizes and tightens the decidability and complexity results obtained in [13].

We evaluate a prototype of our projection algorithm on benchmarks taken from the literature. Our prototype benefits both from the efficiency of existing lightweight but incomplete syntactic projection operators [8,10,11,12] and from the generality of heavyweight automata-based model checking techniques [14,15]: it handles protocols rejected by previous practical approaches while preserving the efficiency that makes MST-based techniques attractive.
